claim: An air-quality gateway that keeps every reading when the uplink drops, tested without hardware.
data_label: simulated data: mock I2C bus, no real sensor
stats: readings kept in order after an outage
limit: Never run on real hardware; the mock proves the gateway logic, not that a real chip answers the same.
alt: Two stacked time series of 30 minutes of simulated room air: CO2 swinging through the ventilate bands and PM2.5 crossing the 15 microgram guideline line.
post:
Your air-quality sensor reads fine on the bench. Then the Wi-Fi drops for an hour and you lose the one stretch of data you cared about.

I built a small open-source edge gateway for indoor air quality. It reads particle, VOC, NOx and CO2 sensors over I2C, works out dew point, absolute humidity and a PM2.5 mean, and ships it over MQTT, InfluxDB or HTTP. Anything bound for HTTP goes into a SQLite queue first and is deleted only after a 2xx.

There is no hardware needed: a mock I2C bus sits underneath the real sensor drivers, so command building and CRC checking run in every test and demo.

Measured on that mock setup: with the uplink port closed I sent three records, brought a server up, and all four arrived in order. The compact uplink payload is 12 bytes, small enough for LoRaWAN, and a generic JS decoder returns the same values as the Python encoder on shared test vectors. 32 Python tests pass in CI.

What is not verified: it has never run on real hardware, so warm-up timing and wiring are untested, and the chart data is simulated.

If you run sensors in the field, what has bitten you hardest: lost uplinks, clock drift, or sensor warm-up?

Code: https://github.com/Usernamepersonperson/airq-edge-gateway
